title: The Address Travels With The Protein

scenes.tts: Make a secretory protein in a test tube with no membranes. It comes out longer than the protein the cell secretes. Why? The extra piece is an address. The cell reads it while the chain is still on the ribosome, then cuts it off once the protein has arrived.
scenes.visual: Two bars: the test-tube product is longer than the secreted one; a question mark marks the missing piece, which turns yellow and is labelled address, then is cut off.
scenes.narration: Make a secretory protein in a test tube with no membranes. It comes out longer than the protein the cell secretes. Why? The extra piece is an address. The cell reads it while the chain is still on the ribosome, then cuts it off once the protein has arrived.

scenes.tts: Almost every protein in a cell starts on a ribosome in the cytosol. That is the fluid outside the organelles. A signal sequence is a stretch of amino acids that carries sorting information. Think of a zip code printed on the parcel. A protein with no signal stays in the cytosol.
scenes.visual: A cell with a ribosome growing a chain in the cytosol; organelle outlines appear; the last beads turn yellow as the signal; a plain chain stays in the cytosol.
scenes.narration: Almost every protein in a cell starts on a ribosome in the cytosol. That is the fluid outside the organelles. A signal sequence is a stretch of amino acids that carries sorting information. Think of a zip code printed on the parcel. A protein with no signal stays in the cytosol.

scenes.tts: For the ER, the address is a hydrophobic stretch, read while the chain is being made. A particle called S R P binds it as it leaves the ribosome. In a wheat germ test tube, S R P halts the growing chain. Then it brings the ribosome to its receptor on the ER membrane.
scenes.caption: For the ER, the address is a hydrophobic stretch, read while the chain is being made. A particle called SRP binds it as it leaves the ribosome. In a wheat germ test tube, SRP halts the growing chain. Then it brings the ribosome to its receptor on the ER membrane.
scenes.visual: Ribosome with a short yellow signal; SRP binds it, the chain halts, and the whole complex moves to the SRP receptor in the ER membrane.
scenes.narration: For the ER, the address is a hydrophobic stretch, read while the chain is being made. A particle called SRP binds it as it leaves the ribosome. In a wheat germ test tube, SRP halts the growing chain. Then it brings the ribosome to its receptor on the ER membrane.

scenes.tts: With G T P bound, S R P and its receptor hold together. They pass the ribosome to the Sec sixty-one channel, which is the pore into the ER. G T P hydrolysis then separates them, and the chain threads through. On the lumenal side, an enzyme called signal peptidase cuts off the signal. That is the extra piece the test tube left on.
scenes.caption: With GTP bound, SRP and its receptor hold together. They pass the ribosome to the Sec61 channel, which is the pore into the ER. GTP hydrolysis then separates them, and the chain threads through. On the lumenal side, an enzyme called signal peptidase cuts off the signal. That is the extra piece the test tube left on.
scenes.visual: GTP badges lock SRP to its receptor; the ribosome moves to Sec61, SRP lets go, the chain threads into the lumen and signal peptidase cuts the yellow piece off.
scenes.narration: With GTP bound, SRP and its receptor hold together. They pass the ribosome to the Sec61 channel, which is the pore into the ER. GTP hydrolysis then separates them, and the chain threads through. On the lumenal side, an enzyme called signal peptidase cuts off the signal. That is the extra piece the test tube left on.

scenes.tts: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes read chains that are already finished. A peroxisomal address is usually a tripeptide at the carboxyl end, such as S K L. Join the first fifty-three residues of a yeast mitochondrial precursor to a mouse enzyme, and the fusion enters yeast mitochondria. Add S K L to the end of a bacterial enzyme, and it enters peroxisomes in mammalian cells.
scenes.caption: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes read chains that are already finished. A peroxisomal address is usually a tripeptide at the carboxyl end, such as SKL. Join the first 53 residues of a yeast mitochondrial precursor to a mouse enzyme, and the fusion enters yeast mitochondria. Add SKL to the end of a bacterial enzyme, and it enters peroxisomes in mammalian cells.
scenes.visual: Three organelle outlines; a yellow SKL tag at the end of a chain; a yellow tag joined to a mouse enzyme carries it into mitochondria; SKL added to a bacterial enzyme carries it into a peroxisome.
scenes.narration: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes read chains that are already finished. A peroxisomal address is usually a tripeptide at the carboxyl end, such as SKL. Join the first 53 residues of a yeast mitochondrial precursor to a mouse enzyme, and the fusion enters yeast mitochondria. Add SKL to the end of a bacterial enzyme, and it enters peroxisomes in mammalian cells.

scenes.tts: So the address is in the protein itself. It is read by a receptor on the organelle. A protein with no signal stays in the cytosol by default. A signal attached to a protein that normally stays there can send it elsewhere. If moving a stretch of sequence moves the protein, that stretch is sufficient to sort it.
scenes.visual: A signalled chain is read by a receptor and enters an organelle; a plain chain stays; a yellow signal attached to the plain chain can send it in; the rule appears.
